title: Lake District
description: Mountainous region and national park in North West England
wiki_lead:
The Lake District, also known as the Lakes or Lakeland, is a mountainous region and national park in Cumbria, North West England. It is famous for its landscape, including its lakes, coast, and mountains, and for its literary associations with Beatrix Potter, John Ruskin, Arthur Ransome, and the Lake Poets.
The Lakeland fells, or mountains, include England's highest: Scafell Pike (978 m; 3,209 ft), Helvellyn (950 m; 3,120 ft) and Skiddaw (931 m; 3,054 ft). The region also contains sixteen major lakes. They include Windermere, which with a length of 11 miles (18 km) and an area of 5.69 square miles (14.73 km2) is the longest and largest lake in England, and Wast Water, which at 79 metres (259 ft) is the deepest lake in England.
The Lake District National Park was established in 1951, and covers an area of 2,362 km2 (912 square miles), the bulk of the region. It was designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2017.

The Lake District, also known as the Lakes or Lakeland, is a mountainous region and national park in Cumbria, North West England. It is famous for its landscape, including its lakes, coast, and mountains, and for its literary associations with Beatrix Potter, John Ruskin, Arthur Ransome, and the Lake Poets.
The Lakeland fells, or mountains, include England's highest: Scafell Pike (978 m; 3,209 ft), Helvellyn (950 m; 3,120 ft) and Skiddaw (931 m; 3,054 ft). The region also contains sixteen major lakes. They include Windermere, which with a length of 11 miles (18 km) and an area of 5.69 square miles (14.73 km2) is the longest and largest lake in England, and Wast Water, which at 79 metres (259 ft) is the deepest lake in England.
The Lake District National Park was established in 1951, and covers an area of 2,362 km2 (912 square miles), the bulk of the region. It was designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2017.


National Park

The Lake District National Park includes all of the central Lake District, though the town of Kendal, some coastal areas and the Cartmel and Furness peninsulas are located outside the park's boundary. The area was designated a national park on 9 May 1951, a month after the Peak District, the first UK national park. It retained its original boundaries until 2016, when it was extended by 3% to the east, in the direction of the Yorkshire Dales National Park, to incorporate land of high landscape value around the Lune Valley.
The national park received 17.73 million tourist visitors in 2024. This equates to 26.85 million tourist days, counting visits of greater than three hours. It is the largest of the thirteen national parks in England and Wales and the second largest in the UK after the Cairngorms National Park. Its aim is to protect the landscape by restricting unwelcome change by industry or commerce. The area of the national park, with the exception of the 2016 extension, was designated a World Heritage Site in 2017 as a cultural landscape. This was the fourth attempt to list the park, after two attempts in the 1980s and one in 2012 failed.
The park is governed by the Lake District National Park Authority, which is based at offices in Kendal. It runs a visitor centre on Windermere at a former country house called Brockhole, Coniston Boating Centre, and information centres. The park authority has 20 members: six appointed by Westmorland and Furness Council, four by Cumberland Council, and ten by the Secretary of State for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs.


Human geography


General

The precise extent of the Lake District is undefined, but it is sometimes considered to be slightly larger than that of the National Park, whose total area is about 2,362 square kilometres (912 sq mi). The park extends just over 51 kilometres (32 mi) from east to west and nearly 64 kilometres (40 mi) from north to south, with areas such as the Lake District Peninsulas to the south lying outside the National Park.


Settlement
There are only a few major settlements within this mountainous area: the towns of Keswick; Windermere and Bowness-on-Windermere (which are contiguous); and Ambleside, are the three largest. The economies of all these are heavily dependent on tourism. Significant settlements close to the boundary of the national park include Carlisle, Barrow-in-Furness, Kendal, Ulverston, Dalton-in-Furness, Whitehaven, Workington, Cockermouth, Penrith, Millom and Grange-over-Sands; each of these has important economic links with the area. Other villages are Coniston, Threlkeld, Glenridding, Pooley Bridge, Broughton-in-Furness, Grasmere, Newby Bridge, Staveley, Lindale, Gosforth and Hawkshead. Beyond these are a scattering of hamlets and many isolated farmsteads, some of which are still tied to agriculture; others now function as part of the tourist economy.

grok_lead: The Lake District National Park is England 's largest national park, encompassing 2,362 square kilometers (912 square miles) in the county of Cumbria in northwest England, and is celebrated for its dramatic glacial landscapes, including sixteen major lakes, rugged fells, and ancient woodlands, which form a unique cultural and natural heritage recognized as a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2017. The park stretches approximately 58 kilometers (36 miles) from west to east and 64 kilometers (40 miles) from north to south, providing a haven for biodiversity with habitats ranging from upland heaths to lowland meadows, and supporting a resident population of around 39,000 people living at a low density of 16.5 per square kilometer. Geographically, the Lake District is defined by its complex geology of volcanic and sedimentary rocks shaped by Ice Age glaciers, resulting in iconic features such as the deepest lake, Wastwater, and the highest peak, Scafell Pike at 978 meters, alongside other prominent mountains like Scafell (964 meters) and Helvellyn (950 meters). The largest lakes include Windermere (14.8 square kilometers), Ullswater (8.9 square kilometers), and Derwentwater (5.5 square kilometers), which together create a mosaic of aquatic and terrestrial ecosystems that sustain diverse wildlife, including rare species in designated Sites of Special Scientific Interest covering nearly a quarter (556 kmÂ²) of the park. These natural elements are interwoven with human-modified landscapes, such as dry-stone walls and traditional farmsteads, reflecting centuries of agricultural and industrial activity that contribute to its status as a world-class cultural landscape. Historically, the Lake District's appreciation as a place of beauty was championed by Romantic poets like William Wordsworth in the 19th century, influencing public campaigns for its protection amid growing industrialization and tourism pressures. Designated as a national park on May 9, 1951, under the National Parks and Access to the Countryside Act 1949, it was established to conserve and enhance its natural beauty, wildlife, and cultural heritage while promoting opportunities for public enjoyment. The park's boundaries were extended in 2016 to include areas like the Kent Estuary, and its UNESCO inscription in 2017 highlighted its global significance as a pioneering example of landscape conservation inspired by 19th-century Romantic ideals. Rich archaeological sites, including prehistoric settlements and Roman frontiers, alongside a distinctive built heritage of stone buildings and conservation areas, underscore its layered human history. Today, the Lake District attracts approximately 18 million visitors annually as of 2023 (17.73 million in 2024), generating Â£2.3 billion in economic value through tourism as of 2023, though recent post-pandemic trends show a decline in numbers and revenue; tourism focuses on walking (with 3,105 kilometers of trails), boating, and cultural experiences in villages like Keswick and Ambleside, while fostering local economic and social well-being. Managed by the Lake District National Park Authority in partnership with 22 organizations, including the National Trust, it addresses challenges such as climate change impacts on habitats, declining agricultural support, and path erosion to maintain its moderate overall condition across cultural and natural assets.
